```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: van Groen BD, Vaes WH, Park BK, Krekels EHJ, van Duijn E,
  Korgvee LT, Maruszak W, Grynkiewicz G, Garner RC, Knibbe CAJ, Tibboel D,
  de Wildt SN, Turner MA. Dose-linearity of the pharmacokinetics of an
  intravenous [14C]midazolam microdose in children. Br J Clin Pharmacol.
  2019;85(10):2332-2340. doi:10.1111/bcp.14047.
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.14047> (open access,
  PMC6783587).
* No erratum or correction notice was found (checked 2026-11-26).

The paper gave a [14C]midazolam microdose (111 Bq/kg, 37.6 ng/kg, infused
over 30 min) to 15 infants on intensive care, either on its own (microdose)
or mixed into a therapeutic midazolam loading dose (microtracer). Plasma
[14C]midazolam was measured by accelerator mass spectrometry and fitted with
a two-compartment model in NONMEM 7.4. Treatment arm had no significant
effect on any parameter, which is the paper's evidence for dose linearity, so
one model describes both arms.

```{r load-model}
mod <- readModelDb("vanGroen_2019_midazolam")
mod_ui <- rxode2::rxode2(mod)
```

The model is on the radioactivity scale the authors fitted: doses in Bq,
[14C]midazolam concentrations in Bq/L (Figures 2-4 axes). The specific
activity of 2.95 MBq/mg (Methods, Radiopharmaceutical preparation) converts
to mass: 1 ng = 2.95 Bq, so 111 Bq/kg = 37.6 ng/kg.

```{r constants}
bq_per_ng <- 2.95 # Methods: specific activity 2.95 MBq/mg = 2.95 Bq/ng
dose_bq_per_kg <- 111 # Methods, Study procedures
dose_bq_per_kg / bq_per_ng # 37.6 ng/kg, as printed
```

# Population

Fifteen infants (Table 1): 9 microdose, 6 microtracer. Gestational age at
birth 39.4 (23.9-41.4) weeks, postnatal age 11.4 (0.6-49.1) weeks, body
weight 3.6 (2.6-8.9) kg, plasma creatinine 35 (20-51) umol/L, total
bilirubin 9 (2-274) umol/L, ASAT 42 (12-93) U/L, ALAT 17 (7-68) U/L (median
(range)). Up to 5 samples per infant between 0.17 and 36 h; 59 of 67 samples
were above the detection limit and modelled. Sex and race were not reported.
Infants with serious hepatic or renal impairment, haemofiltration, dialysis
or ECMO were excluded.

# Source trace

| Element | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | 2-compartment, IV input | Results, Nonlinear mixed effects modelling; Table 3 |
| `lcl` | log(2.06 L/h) | Table 3, CL |
| `lq` | log(0.79 L/h) | Table 3, Q |
| `lvc` | log(3.81 L) at 4 kg | Table 3, V1_4kg |
| `e_wt_vc` | 1.36 | Table 3, k1 in V1i = V1_4kg x (WT/4)^k1 |
| `lvp` | log(3.19 L) | Table 3, V2 |
| `etalcl` | 0.73 (variance) | Table 3, omega2 CL |
| `propSd` | sqrt(0.09) = 0.30 | Table 3, Proportional error (variance; see below) |
| `addSd` | sqrt(0.08) = 0.283 Bq/L | Table 3, Additional error (variance; see below) |
| Dose | 111 Bq/kg over 30 min | Methods, Study procedures |
| Units | Bq, Bq/L, h | Figures 2-4 axes; Table 3 |

## Residual error: variances, not SDs

Table 3 labels the IIV row `omega2` but gives the residual rows no symbol.
Three pieces of evidence put them on the NONMEM `$SIGMA` (variance) scale:

1. **Bootstrap interval width.** For `N` observations the relative width of
   a 95% interval is about `3.92 * sqrt(2/N)` for a variance and half that
   for an SD. With 59 modelled observations the proportional row's
   bootstrap interval is wider than both predictions and nearer the variance
   one (computed below).
2. **Figure 4B scatter.** Observed versus individual predictions in the
   10-100 Bq/L range deviate by 30-50% for several samples. An SD of 0.09
   (9%) would make those 4-5 SD residuals; an SD of 0.30 makes them ordinary.
3. **Low concentrations.** At individual predictions near 0.1-0.3 Bq/L
   Figure 4B shows observations of 0.45 and 0.09 Bq/L. An additive SD of
   0.08 Bq/L would make these 3-4 SD residuals; sqrt(0.08) = 0.28 Bq/L
   covers them, and is about the 0.31 Bq/L quantification limit.

```{r sigma-scale}
n_obs <- 67 - 8
prop_boot <- c(median = 0.08, lo = 0.05, hi = 0.14) # Table 3 bootstrap
data.frame(
  observed = unname((prop_boot["hi"] - prop_boot["lo"]) / prop_boot["median"]),
  if_variance = 3.92 * sqrt(2 / n_obs),
  if_sd = 3.92 * sqrt(1 / (2 * n_obs))
) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Observed relative width" = observed,
    "Predicted if variance" = if_variance,
    "Predicted if SD" = if_sd
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Relative width of the proportional-error bootstrap interval.")
```

## Closed-form check against the Discussion

The Discussion restates the clearance for a 4 kg infant as 8.6 mL/kg/min.

```{r cl-check}
cl_typ <- exp(mod_ui$theta[["lcl"]])
cl_ml_kg_min <- cl_typ / 4 * 1000 / 60
cl_ml_kg_min
stopifnot(abs(cl_ml_kg_min - 8.6) < 0.05)
```

# Virtual cohort

Body weight is the only covariate. Weights are drawn from a log-normal
distribution with the Table 1 median (3.6 kg), truncated to the observed
2.6-8.9 kg range. Each infant gets 111 Bq/kg over 30 min.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(2019)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2019)
n_sub <- 200
wt <- numeric(0)
while (length(wt) < n_sub) {
  draw <- exp(rnorm(n_sub, log(3.6), 0.35))
  wt <- c(wt, draw[draw >= 2.6 & draw <= 8.9])
}
cohort <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n_sub), WT = wt[seq_len(n_sub)])
summary(cohort$WT)

obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 1, by = 0.05), seq(1.25, 36, by = 0.25))))

dose_rows <- cohort |>
  mutate(
    time = 0, amt = dose_bq_per_kg * WT, dur = 0.5,
    evid = 1L, cmt = "central"
  )
obs_rows <- cohort |>
  tidyr::crossing(time = obs_times) |>
  mutate(amt = 0, dur = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central")
events <- bind_rows(dose_rows, obs_rows) |>
  arrange(id, time, desc(evid)) |>
  mutate(treatment = "microdose or microtracer")
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate, warning = FALSE}
sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events, keep = c("WT", "treatment")) |>
  as.data.frame()
sim_typ <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  rxode2::zeroRe(mod),
  bind_rows(
    lapply(c(2.6, 3.6, 8.9), function(w) {
      data.frame(
        id = w, WT = w,
        time = c(0, obs_times), amt = c(dose_bq_per_kg * w, rep(0, length(obs_times))),
        dur = c(0.5, rep(0, length(obs_times))), evid = c(1L, rep(0L, length(obs_times))),
        cmt = "central"
      )
    })
  ),
  keep = "WT"
) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

## Concentration-time profiles

Replicates the scale and shape of Figures 2 and 3 of van Groen 2019
(individual semilog [14C]midazolam profiles, about 100-150 Bq/L shortly after
the infusion and 0.1-10 Bq/L by 12-36 h).

```{r fig-vpc}
vpc <- sim |>
  filter(time > 0) |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(
    p05 = quantile(sim, 0.05), p50 = quantile(sim, 0.5), p95 = quantile(sim, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # The additive error makes the lower percentile negative late in the
  # profile; floor it for the log axis, well below the 0.31 Bq/L LLOQ.
  mutate(p05 = pmax(p05, 0.05))
ggplot(vpc, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p50)) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(sim_typ, time > 0),
    aes(y = Cc, colour = factor(WT)), linetype = 2
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Time after start of infusion (h)", y = "[14C]midazolam (Bq/L)",
    colour = "Typical infant WT (kg)",
    caption = "Ribbon: 5th-95th percentile of 200 simulated infants with residual error\n(floored at 0.05 Bq/L); solid line: median."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

## Typical-value profiles by weight

Weight changes only the central volume. With a per-kg dose the amount rises
in proportion to weight and the central volume as WT^1.36, so heavier infants
have a slightly lower peak; clearance does not scale with weight, so AUC
rises in proportion to weight.

```{r fig-typ}
ggplot(filter(sim_typ, time > 0), aes(time, Cc, colour = factor(WT))) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "[14C]midazolam (Bq/L)", colour = "WT (kg)") +
  theme_bw()
```

# PKNCA validation

NCA on the simulated profiles, converted to mass units (ng/L) for
comparison with Table 2.

```{r pknca}
conc_df <- sim |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  transmute(id, treatment, time, conc = Cc / bq_per_ng)
dose_df <- dose_rows |>
  transmute(id, treatment = "microdose or microtracer", time, dose = amt / bq_per_ng)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_df, conc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, dose ~ time | treatment + id, duration = 0.5, route = "intravascular")
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0, end = Inf, cmax = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE, half.life = TRUE
)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))
nca_long <- as.data.frame(nca_res)
```

## Comparison against the published NCA

Table 2 reports median AUC0-inf of 48.90 ng.h/L (range 34.15-218.80; total
cohort, n = 14) from a log-linear NCA of the 2-5 observed samples per
infant.

```{r nca-compare}
published <- data.frame(treatment = "microdose or microtracer", aucinf.obs = 48.90)
cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca_long,
  reference = published,
  by = "treatment",
  params = "aucinf.obs",
  units = c(aucinf.obs = "ng*h/L"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
cmp |>
  dplyr::rename("Group" = treatment) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    caption = "Simulated (median of 200 infants, dense sampling) vs van Groen 2019 Table 2 median AUC0-inf."
  )

auc_sim <- nca_long |> filter(PPTESTCD == "aucinf.obs") |> pull(PPORRES)
quantile(auc_sim, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

The simulated median AUC0-inf is about 45% above the published NCA median,
and the gap comes from the paper's own estimates, not from the simulation. A
typical 3.6 kg infant receives 37.6 x 3.6 = 135 ng and the model's typical
clearance is 2.06 L/h, so its AUC is about 66 ng.h/L (the simulated median is
a little higher because the weight distribution is right-skewed).
Reproducing a median of 48.9 ng.h/L would need a clearance near 2.8 L/h,
which is inside the bootstrap interval for CL (1.57-3.23 L/h). Two features
of the study make a gap of this size unremarkable:

* the published median is over only 14 infants, and with a clearance
  variance of 0.73 the standard error of that median is roughly
  1.25 x sqrt(0.73) / sqrt(14), about 0.29 on the log scale (+/- 33%);
* the NCA used 2-5 samples per infant, several last sampled at 2-4 h
  (Figure 2), so the log-linear extrapolation often used the steeper
  distribution phase and underestimated AUC0-inf.

The simulated 5th-95th percentile range overlaps the published range
(34-219 ng.h/L). No parameter was adjusted to close the gap.

```{r nca-gate}
auc_typ <- 37.6 * 3.6 / 2.06
stopifnot(
  # The simulated median is dose / CL for a typical infant; a dose-unit or
  # clearance transcription error would move it by far more than the weight
  # skew and the sampling error of a 200-infant median.
  abs(median(auc_sim) / auc_typ - 1) < 0.3,
  # The simulated central 90% overlaps the published individual range.
  quantile(auc_sim, 0.05) < 218.8,
  quantile(auc_sim, 0.95) > 34.15
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Residual-error scale.** Table 3 gives the residual rows without a
  symbol. They are read as NONMEM `$SIGMA` variances (proportional SD 0.30,
  additive SD 0.283 Bq/L); the evidence is set out above.
* **Units.** The model was fitted on the radioactivity scale (Figures 2-4 in
  Bq/L) and is packaged on that scale; doses are in Bq. Multiply by
  1/2.95 to convert Bq to ng of midazolam. The additive error is in Bq/L and
  would need the same conversion if concentrations were modelled in ng/L.
* **Microdose and microtracer.** The paper found no effect of treatment arm
  on any parameter, and the model has no arm covariate. Only the labelled
  [14C]midazolam is modelled; the unlabelled therapeutic midazolam given with
  the microtracer is not part of the model.
* **1-hydroxy-midazolam.** The metabolite was analysed only by NCA (Table 2);
  there is no metabolite model to extract.
* **Virtual cohort.** Weight is log-normal around the Table 1 median and
  truncated to the observed range; the paper reports only median and range.
* **Covariates screened but not retained** (postnatal and postmenstrual age,
  creatinine, ALAT, ASAT, total bilirubin, treatment arm) are listed in the
  model's `covariatesDataExcluded`; the paper gives no estimates for them.
